new_statements.quote: If only bi-syllabic words are taken into account, the prosodic phenomena can be described as contrastive stress. However, on monosyllabic words Bromley found three contrastive pitch patterns: 1. short low or downglide; 2. short and high; 3. long upgliding high. The three tone patterns are more clearly recognisable in the Tiau dialect than in the Senggo dialect, Bromley observed. [p. 37] ... Recently M. Bromley found in Citak Asmat evidence for a tonal system restricted to monosyllabic words, bi-syllabics having phonemic stress (see chapter 5, section 2). [p. 22]

new_statements.rule_in_words: For Citak Asmat (not Diuwe proper): stress in bisyllabic words is contrastive, i.e. lexically unpredictable (phonemic stress), while monosyllables carry one of three contrastive pitch/length patterns; a tonal system restricted to monosyllables coexisting with phonemic stress in polysyllables. No placement rule is given.
new_statements.exceptions: Tone contrasts are clearer in Tiau than in Senggo; in Senggo part of the speakers no longer distinguish patterns 1 and 2 by pitch, keeping instead a length contrast (1,2 vs 3) or a 'ballistic'-onset contrast (footnote 35, Bromley p.c.).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (bisyllabic vs monosyllabic words, Citak Asmat Senggo/Tiau dialects). Explicitly a 'tentative' analysis 'by no means final'. Nothing is said about Diuwe/Brazza itself; Diuwe's only link is Voorhoeve's p. 36 remark that the Upper Sirec and Brazza River short lists 'seem to represent dialects of Citak Asmat (Van Arsdale 1975:18)'.
new_statements.first_reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.identity_note: Diuwe [diuw1238, diy] has no linguistic description of its own (Glottolog Glottolog's most extensive description: Van Arsdale 1974, a wordlist or less). Hammarström's bibliography equates it with the 'Brazza' (River) group of Van Arsdale 1974/1987 and Mitton 1983; Voorhoeve 1980:36 says the Upper Sirec (list 83) and Brazza River (list 84) short lists 'seem to represent dialects of Citak Asmat (Van Arsdale 1975:18)'; Glottolog 5.3 places Diuwe in the family node Citak Asmat [cita1246] with Citak [cita1245] and Tamnim Citak [tamn1235]; Wikipedia states 'Diuwe is unverified as a language'. The stress/tone statement quoted concerns Citak [cita1245], Senggo and Tiau dialects, as reported by Voorhoeve from Bromley's unpublished analysis, so it belongs, if anywhere, under cita1245 with a second-hand flag, not under diuw1238.
